title: The Design Problem
visual: First-person approach to a flush walnut door with an ambiguous steel disc; push fails twice; pull opens it; freeze; orbit; amber point emerges; dip to the time corridor; main title.
narration: A door stands before you. There is no clear handle, so you push. Nothing. You pull. It opens. You feel foolish. But what if the problem was never you? What if it was the design? That tiny moment reveals the question behind user experience: can a product make sense to a human being?

title: Before Screens — Human Factors
visual: Point becomes a toggle-switch lamp; tracking shot along a mid-century control panel; rotary telephone; confusable levers vs shape-coded fix with measurement guides; Dreyfuss lower third and book reconstruction; dial becomes an input wheel.
visual_category: Illustrative reconstructions (panel, telephone, book spine text)
narration: Long before apps, people struggled with tools, machines, and everyday objects. During the twentieth century, industrial designers and human-factors researchers began asking how controls should fit human bodies and minds. In 1955, Henry Dreyfuss published Designing for People, bringing measurements, observation, and testing into the design conversation. Think telephone dials, cockpit switches, and confusing appliances. Good design was becoming less about the machine alone, and more about the person using it.

title: The Mouse Changes Everything
visual: 1968 auditorium; projection screen with structured text, link following, editing, split-screen collaboration; mouse/cursor close-ups; 1964 wooden prototype (one button) vs 1968 three-button demo mouse; cursor into a window.
historical_basis: 9 Dec 1968 demo; 1964 prototype built by Bill English (verified)
narration: In 1968, Douglas Engelbart and his team stunned an audience with what we now call the Mother of All Demos. They showed a mouse, linked documents, on-screen editing, and collaboration, long before those ideas felt ordinary. The mouse itself had emerged from experiments earlier in the decade; a wooden prototype came in 1964. But the famous 1968 demonstration used a later model. Computing began to feel like something you could point to, not simply program.

title: The Graphical Revolution

narration: In 1973, Xerox PARC built the Alto, bringing graphical displays, windows, and the mouse into one experimental machine. Xerox's Star followed in 1981 with a more complete desktop metaphor. Complex systems borrowed the language of everyday life.

title: The Web and the Name UX
visual: Book reconstruction (POET 1988); NeXT cube at CERN; 1989 proposal; first website page reconstruction (Dec 1990/Aug 1991); link into a 3D document network; 1993 'user experience' at Apple; INTERFACE→PRODUCT→SERVICE→EXPERIENCE diagram.
narration: In 1988, Don Norman explained why everyday objects confuse us. A year later, Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN. By 1991, its first website made linked information navigable. The question now reached beyond operating a machine: could people find what they needed, and feel confident doing it? In 1993, Norman helped establish 'user experience' as a professional term at Apple. That experience extended far beyond the screen.

title: The Web Goes Mobile
visual: Crowded 1990s page with annotated problems → clearer structure; WCAG 1.0 (1999) keyboard-focus path; 2007 touchscreen phone reconstruction with tap/flick/pinch; 2010 responsive layout reflowing across three devices.
narration: As websites multiplied, navigation, readability, trust, and speed began to matter as much as appearance. Accessibility gained shared standards, including the first Web Content Accessibility Guidelines in 1999. Then, in 2007, the iPhone made touching, flicking, and pinching central to a mainstream mobile interface. In 2010, responsive web design offered a way for layouts to adapt to different screens. The interface no longer belonged to one desk or one kind of user.

title: UX vs UI — The Big Reveal
visual: Fictional shop: beautiful UI, hidden delivery cost at the last step; freeze 'BEAUTIFUL UI. FRUSTRATING UX.'; layers of the journey; RESEARCH→DEFINE→IDEATE→PROTOTYPE→TEST→ITERATE; usability observation; redesign; before/after.
narration: So what exactly are UX and UI? UI, or user interface, is the layer of controls and feedback: buttons, labels, sounds, color, and interaction patterns. UX, or user experience, is the broader journey: can someone understand it, complete a task, trust the result, and feel in control? Imagine a stunning checkout page that hides the delivery cost until the end. Beautiful UI; frustrating UX. Designers research real needs, map journeys, sketch options, prototype interactions, and test with people. Then they revise. Great experiences are not born from guessing. They are improved by observing.

title: Design for Everyone
visual: Collaborative canvas with tokens → components → consistent screens; browser-based tools (2010s; Figma 2016); accessibility: focus, text, labels, contrast, error messages, reduced motion, input methods; WCAG 2.2 (2023); helpful vs manipulative choice.
narration: Today, designers collaborate and use shared components and design systems to keep products consistent. Browser-based tools allow teams to design together. But progress is not just faster software. It is readable text, keyboard access, clear error recovery, and choices that respect attention and privacy. Standards such as WCAG 2.2 advance inclusion. What counts is not how polished a screen looks, but who it works for, and who it leaves out.

title: The Next Interface
visual: Point becomes a voice waveform; grounded assistant reply; AI conversation cards; spatial panels (labelled speculative); collapse to the point; backwards through the corridor; the same door with a clear pull bar opens first time; soft light; closing cards.
narration: Now interfaces are changing again: conversations with AI, voice commands, spatial computing, and experiences that may not look like screens at all. The tools will change. The responsibility will not. Find the human problem. Design with people, not assumptions. Test what you have made. And remember that door? When it finally opens the way you expect, you barely notice the design. That is often the point.
